title: Why softer food prices and slower wages did not stop a September hike
summary: The 25-basis-point increase announced in Berlin on 10 September came despite lower-than-expected prices in some areas and little evidence that wages had responded to the energy shock. The relevant revision concerned duration. Staff kept their 2026 headline inflation forecast at 3.0% and raised it for 2027 and 2028. Consumption and public spending had held up better than expected, leaving more scope for firms to pass on sustained energy costs. The Governing Council was unanimous about the move at this meeting. Lagarde said members had not debated which way rates should move next. A reporter’s description of several further increases in market pricing was put to her as a question, and she declined to validate it (opening statement and first two Q&A exchanges).

August’s consumer price index showed how the price of energy actually reached the household. Headline inflation rose from 2.9% in July to 3.3% in August, and energy inflation rose from 10.3% to 14.3%. Beyond higher raw commodity prices, the ECB pointed to widening refining margins on liquid fuel. The price of crude and the price of usable diesel can move differently when refining becomes a bottleneck. At the same time food inflation held at 1.2%, goods inflation rose from 0.9% to 1.2% and services slowed from 3.3% to 3.0%. Inflation excluding food and energy edged down from 2.5% to 2.4%. Investors seeing a steep increase in headline inflation and slower underlying inflation thus had to decide which was more informative about the part of the shock yet to reach borrowers and consumers (‘Inflation’ and Q&A on refining margins).

Food was a revealing test of that distinction. Processed-food prices increased less than unprocessed-food prices. Lagarde identified favourable weather early in the year, contained increases in costs such as labour and transport entering processed food, and anecdotal signs that consumers changed the products they bought. The last mechanism could limit a supplier’s ability to pass on costs even when input prices were higher. It was not captured in a single index. The staff projection still incorporated higher food prices ahead on the assumption that a persistent energy shock would gradually reach production and distribution. The informative evidence would be how often suppliers revised prices and whether consumers continued to substitute cheaper products. A low current reading alone could not settle the matter (Q&A on food pricing).

The labour numbers were more reassuring about immediate propagation. Compensation per employee grew 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.5% in the first. A pickup in productivity helped slow unit labour-cost growth from 3.5% to 2.6%. Growth in unit profits, however, increased from 0.3% to 2.2%. Firms’ earnings per unit of output and employees’ compensation per unit of output were moving differently, so taking wage growth as a proxy for all domestic cost pressure would be misleading. The wage tracker pointed to a modest pickup in negotiated pay growth to 2.7% in the first half of 2027. Short-horizon inflation expectations remained elevated, while most longer-horizon measures were around 2%. The Council could respond to the prospect of more persistent inflation before observing a wage-price feedback loop (‘Inflation’).

The projected paths for headline and core inflation diverged beyond the current year. Over 2026–28, headline inflation averaged 3.0%, 2.5% and 2.1%, while inflation excluding food and energy averaged 2.5%, 2.6% and 2.3%. Staff expected headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027. Energy inflation would subsequently turn negative up to mid-2028, supporting a return to around target toward the end of 2027. Meanwhile core inflation would keep rising until early 2027, stay elevated for the rest of that year and moderate in 2028. A decline in the headline rate in that sequence would initially exaggerate the improvement in underlying inflation. Lagarde said the September increase stood up in all three of the updated benign, adverse and severe scenarios. An individual gas price quoted by a journalist was insufficient to identify which complete scenario the economy had entered (‘Inflation’ and Q&A on the adverse gas scenario).

There was a second forecast question involving the date on which growth information became available. Staff projected growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028. The upward revisions to 2026 and 2027 reflected more resilient private consumption and public spending. Manufacturing benefited from defence and infrastructure spending. Confidence had recovered, while AI activity contributed to digital services, investment and exports. Unemployment was 6.4% in July as workforce and employment growth slowed and productivity picked up. Second-quarter growth of 0.6% became available after the forecast cut-off. Lagarde said using it would imply more than 0.9% growth in 2026. She did not supply a replacement staff forecast. The published vintage and the later piece of news belong in separate observations in a historical record (‘Economic activity’ and answer on the two forecast surprises).

The June hike had begun to reach private financing. New bank lending rates for firms had risen from 3.6% in May to 3.8% in both June and July. Corporate bank loan balances nevertheless grew 4.4% year on year in July after 4.0% in May and June. Lagarde’s statement stressed the slower response of loan quantities. Market-based borrowing cost 4.0% in July, little changed recently but well above its pre-conflict level. Annual corporate bond issuance growth was 3.4% in July after 3.6% in June, while mortgage rates held at 3.5% and mortgage lending growth eased to 3.0%. An estimate of aggregate stimulus based only on the most recent corporate loan stock would miss tighter prices for new loans and weaker mortgage volume growth (‘Financial and monetary conditions’).

Longer-dated bond yields had risen across global markets since July. Lagarde discussed several possible influences, including financing demand from AI-related activities extending from equities into bonds and private credit, and spillovers from the large US market. She said global yields entered the staff projections and were being monitored, particularly at the long end. She offered no attribution of the change in euro yields among those factors. Asked about sovereign spreads, she declined to label a particular widening as fragmentation. The quantity of central-bank liquidity was changing too. In the final exchange she cited a decline from €4.7 trillion to €2.1 trillion as the Eurosystem allowed bonds to mature without replacing them. Those figures described a broader adjustment and carried no claim about the size of the change since July. For event studies, worldwide long-rate movements, a gradual balance-sheet runoff and a current 25-basis-point policy decision operate on different clocks (Q&A on global yields, sovereign spreads and the balance sheet).

The policy uncertainty consequently lay in the pace and channels of transmission, rather than in disagreement about the day’s hike. Staff’s estimates of a neutral-rate band had limited weight in the decision because that rate is hard to identify during repeated shocks. The Council retained its discretion to move in either direction as the combination of inflation, growth and financing conditions evolved. The published conference provides evidence about why the ECB acted and what it monitored. Establishing how much of that reasoning surprised investors would require prices immediately before and after both the announcement and the answers in Berlin (Q&A on the neutral rate and policy path).

questions.question: Was the policy news concentrated at the next few meetings or in the expected longer-run rate?
questions.detail: Compare meeting-dated overnight-indexed swap changes with longer forwards around the statement and Q&A, checking international yields and energy prices in the same windows. The meeting disclosed a unanimous hike but gave no terminal rate. A global long-end move and a change in expected ECB decisions carry different duration exposures.

questions.question: How much persistence did refining and food-price transmission add?
questions.detail: Match crude and refined-product prices, gas costs and refining margins to transport and manufacturing inputs. Follow producer and retail food prices separately for processed and unprocessed products, allowing for weather and substitution. The frequency of actual price resets could distinguish delayed pass-through from suppliers absorbing a durable margin squeeze.

questions.question: Did the inflation composition evolve as forecast once energy inflation fell?
questions.detail: Compare core inflation, services, compensation, productivity and unit profits with the September vintage. Attribute changes in headline inflation to energy separately. If headline inflation approached target only because energy subtracted from it, the projected persistence in underlying prices would remain important for real yields and the policy outlook.

questions.question: How long did the June rate increase take to reach borrowers’ spending?
questions.detail: Compare new loan pricing with subsequent drawdowns, loan demand, corporate bond issuance and household mortgage activity, matching release dates to the information available at each meeting. Already rising loan rates alongside accelerating corporate loan balances provide a starting point for distinguishing a lagged quantity response from continuing strength in spending.
